name: Malachite
poem: A rich mineral green born when copper meets water and time — banded, polished, mined for the eyeshadow of pharaohs and the parlours of tsars.

recipe.note: A rich mineral green, cool and slightly bluish.

lenses.label: Art History
lenses.intro: Ground malachite gave Egyptian, Russian and Chinese painters their first stable, brilliant green — and the rock itself was carved into furniture for emperors.

entries.title: The Tomb of Nefertari
entries.meta: Valley of the Queens · c. 1290 BC
entries.blurb: Nefertari's tomb walls are painted with crushed malachite for plant life and Hathor's headdress — the colour has stayed vivid for three thousand years.

entries.title: The Malachite Room
entries.blurb: Two metric tons of Ural malachite carved into panels and pillars by Nicholas I's court — a single room with more malachite than most museum collections.

entries.title: Song Dynasty Landscapes
entries.blurb: The green of distant mountains in Chinese blue-and-green landscape painting is malachite — ground fine, suspended in glue, painted in thin glazing layers.

lenses.label: Fashion
lenses.intro: Malachite has rarely appeared in textiles — but its shaped, polished form has dominated jewellery and decorative dress for five millennia.

entries.title: Egyptian Eye Makeup
entries.blurb: Ground malachite was the green half of the Egyptian eye paint kit (alongside kohl) — applied with bone sticks, partly for beauty and partly to repel flies.

entries.title: Russian Imperial Jewellery
entries.blurb: Fabergé carved Ural malachite into eggs, pen rests, and brooches — the stone's natural banding made every piece unique, a colour that imitates nothing.

entries.title: Art Deco Brooches
entries.blurb: Art Deco jewellers paired polished malachite cabochons with chrome and onyx — the saturated green reading as both ancient and machine-age modern at once.

lenses.label: Nature
lenses.intro: Malachite forms where copper-bearing rocks meet groundwater — slowly, layer by layer, in concentric green bands.

entries.title: Malachite Ore
entries.blurb: The mineral forms in caverns and fractures of weathered copper deposits — every cross-section reveals concentric banding, the geological equivalent of tree rings.

entries.title: The Ural Mountains
entries.blurb: The greatest malachite deposits ever found — boulders weighing tens of tons. The mines that supplied Catherine and Nicholas have been worked dry.

entries.title: The Malachite Sunbird
entries.blurb: An African sunbird whose males blaze the exact iridescent green-blue of polished malachite — coincidence, not pigment chemistry: the bird's colour comes from feather structure.

lenses.label: Pop Culture
lenses.intro: Malachite has stayed quietly iconic — a colour that pops up wherever cultures want to signal old wealth or natural luxury.

entries.title: The Crystal Healing Industry
entries.blurb: Malachite is among the most-sold tumbled stones in the crystal trade — sold for "protection" and "transformation," with no scientific basis but enduring appeal.

entries.title: Tom Ford Malachite
entries.blurb: The colour returned to its predynastic Egyptian role — premium eyeshadow palettes still feature "Malachite" as a benchmark green tone, often containing none of the mineral.

entries.title: Cartier Panthère
entries.blurb: The signature Cartier panther's eyes are set with cabochon malachite — a design detail Jeanne Toussaint introduced in the 1940s that has never been altered.

lenses.label: Etymology
lenses.intro: The stone's name comes from a plant — the Greeks named the colour after a leaf, then forgot the leaf and kept the name.

entries.title: "Malachē"
entries.blurb: The leaves of the mallow plant are exactly the green of malachite. The Greeks named the stone for the leaf — the only common-knowledge match they had.

entries.title: "Molochites"
entries.blurb: Pliny's Natural History records the stone under its Latinised name — already an export trade across the empire, mined in Sinai and Cyprus.

entries.title: "Mountain Green"
entries.blurb: The Chinese name keeps the geological reality — the colour came from grinding stone, and the colour was the colour of distant mountains.

lenses.label: Symbolism
lenses.intro: Malachite's symbolism splits neatly between two roles: the protector and the transformer.

entries.title: The Eye of Horus
entries.blurb: Powdered malachite outlined the eyes of mummies as well as the living — a literal third eye, painted on the wrapped face to see in the afterlife.

entries.title: The Russian Soul
entries.blurb: Malachite recurs in Pavel Bazhov's Ural folktales as the colour of the Mistress of the Copper Mountain — a Russian Persephone, both terrifying and generous.

entries.title: Transformation
entries.blurb: Malachite's banded growth — copper meeting water, becoming carbonate, becoming green — made it the modern crystal community's symbol for change made visible.
